# lib.rs - source

Source: https://docs.rs/lapin/4.10.0/src/lapin/lib.rs.html

# lapin/lib.rs

[1](https://docs.rs#1)#![deny(missing_docs, missing_debug_implementations, unsafe_code)]
[2](https://docs.rs#2)#![warn(unreachable_pub, unused_qualifications, unused_lifetimes)]
[3](https://docs.rs#3)#![warn(
[4](https://docs.rs#4)    clippy::must_use_candidate,
[5](https://docs.rs#5)    clippy::unwrap_in_result,
[6](https://docs.rs#6)    clippy::panic_in_result_fn
[7](https://docs.rs#7))]
[8](https://docs.rs#8)
[9](https://docs.rs#9)//! An async AMQP 0-9-1 client library targeting RabbitMQ.
[10](https://docs.rs#10)//!
[11](https://docs.rs#11)//! # Core concepts
[12](https://docs.rs#12)//!
[13](https://docs.rs#13)//! **[`Connection`]** — a single TCP socket to the broker. One process
[14](https://docs.rs#14)//! typically creates one connection and reuses it throughout its lifetime.
[15](https://docs.rs#15)//!
[16](https://docs.rs#16)//! **[`Channel`]** — a lightweight virtual connection multiplexed over a
[17](https://docs.rs#17)//! [`Connection`]. All AMQP operations (declaring queues, publishing,
[18](https://docs.rs#18)//! consuming, …) are performed through channels. Open as many as you need;
[19](https://docs.rs#19)//! they are cheap.
[20](https://docs.rs#20)//!
[21](https://docs.rs#21)//! **[`Consumer`]** — an async `Stream` of [`message::Delivery`] values
[22](https://docs.rs#22)//! obtained by calling [`Channel::basic_consume`]. Each delivery must be
[23](https://docs.rs#23)//! explicitly acknowledged once processed.
[24](https://docs.rs#24)//!
[25](https://docs.rs#25)//! **[`PublisherConfirm`]** — a future returned by [`Channel::basic_publish`]
[26](https://docs.rs#26)//! that resolves to a [`Confirmation`] once the broker has acknowledged the
[27](https://docs.rs#27)//! message (requires [`Channel::confirm_select`]).
[28](https://docs.rs#28)//!
[29](https://docs.rs#29)//! # Quick start
[30](https://docs.rs#30)//!
[31](https://docs.rs#31)//! ```rust,no_run
[32](https://docs.rs#32)//! use async_rs::traits::Executor;
[33](https://docs.rs#33)//! use futures_lite::stream::StreamExt;
[34](https://docs.rs#34)//! use lapin::{
[35](https://docs.rs#35)//!     options::*, types::FieldTable, BasicProperties, Connection,
[36](https://docs.rs#36)//!     ConnectionProperties, Result,
[37](https://docs.rs#37)//! };
[38](https://docs.rs#38)//!
[39](https://docs.rs#39)//! fn main() -> Result<()> {
[40](https://docs.rs#40)//!     let addr = std::env::var("AMQP_ADDR")
[41](https://docs.rs#41)//!         .unwrap_or_else(|_| "amqp://127.0.0.1:5672/%2f".into());
[42](https://docs.rs#42)//!     let runtime = lapin::runtime::default_runtime()?;
[43](https://docs.rs#43)//!
[44](https://docs.rs#44)//!     runtime.clone().block_on(async move {
[45](https://docs.rs#45)//!         let conn = Connection::connect(&addr, ConnectionProperties::default()).await?;
[46](https://docs.rs#46)//!
[47](https://docs.rs#47)//!         let channel = conn.create_channel().await?;
[48](https://docs.rs#48)//!
[49](https://docs.rs#49)//!         channel
[50](https://docs.rs#50)//!             .queue_declare("hello".into(), QueueDeclareOptions::durable(), FieldTable::default())
[51](https://docs.rs#51)//!             .await?;
[52](https://docs.rs#52)//!
[53](https://docs.rs#53)//!         channel
[54](https://docs.rs#54)//!             .basic_publish(
[55](https://docs.rs#55)//!                 "".into(),
[56](https://docs.rs#56)//!                 "hello".into(),
[57](https://docs.rs#57)//!                 BasicPublishOptions::default(),
[58](https://docs.rs#58)//!                 b"Hello, world!",
[59](https://docs.rs#59)//!                 BasicProperties::default(),
[60](https://docs.rs#60)//!             )
[61](https://docs.rs#61)//!             .await?
[62](https://docs.rs#62)//!             .await?;
[63](https://docs.rs#63)//!
[64](https://docs.rs#64)//!         let mut consumer = channel
[65](https://docs.rs#65)//!             .basic_consume(
[66](https://docs.rs#66)//!                 "hello".into(),
[67](https://docs.rs#67)//!                 "my_consumer".into(),
[68](https://docs.rs#68)//!                 BasicConsumeOptions::default(),
[69](https://docs.rs#69)//!                 FieldTable::default(),
[70](https://docs.rs#70)//!             )
[71](https://docs.rs#71)//!             .await?;
[72](https://docs.rs#72)//!
[73](https://docs.rs#73)//!         while let Some(delivery) = consumer.next().await {
[74](https://docs.rs#74)//!             let delivery = delivery?;
[75](https://docs.rs#75)//!             delivery.ack(BasicAckOptions::default()).await?;
[76](https://docs.rs#76)//!         }
[77](https://docs.rs#77)//!         Ok(())
[78](https://docs.rs#78)//!     })
[79](https://docs.rs#79)//! }
[80](https://docs.rs#80)//! ```
[81](https://docs.rs#81)//!
[82](https://docs.rs#82)//! # Automatic connection recovery
[83](https://docs.rs#83)//!
[84](https://docs.rs#84)//! Enable recovery in [`ConnectionProperties`] to automatically reconnect and
[85](https://docs.rs#85)//! replay topology (exchanges, queues, bindings, consumers) after a network
[86](https://docs.rs#86)//! failure:
[87](https://docs.rs#87)//!
[88](https://docs.rs#88)//! ```rust,no_run
[89](https://docs.rs#89)//! use lapin::ConnectionProperties;
[90](https://docs.rs#90)//!
[91](https://docs.rs#91)//! let props = ConnectionProperties::default().enable_auto_recover();
[92](https://docs.rs#92)//! // then pass `props` to Connection::connect(…)
[93](https://docs.rs#93)//! ```
[94](https://docs.rs#94)//!
[95](https://docs.rs#95)//! After catching an error from a channel operation, call
[96](https://docs.rs#96)//! [`Channel::wait_for_recovery`] to block until the connection has been
[97](https://docs.rs#97)//! re-established:
[98](https://docs.rs#98)//!
[99](https://docs.rs#99)//! ```rust,no_run
[100](https://docs.rs#100)//! # use lapin::{Channel, Error, Result};
[101](https://docs.rs#101)//! # async fn example(channel: Channel, error: Error) -> Result<()> {
[102](https://docs.rs#102)//! channel.wait_for_recovery(error).await?;
[103](https://docs.rs#103)//! # Ok(())
[104](https://docs.rs#104)//! # }
[105](https://docs.rs#105)//! ```
[106](https://docs.rs#106)//!
[107](https://docs.rs#107)//! # Feature flags
[108](https://docs.rs#108)//!
[109](https://docs.rs#109)//! ## Async runtime (pick exactly one)
[110](https://docs.rs#110)//!
[111](https://docs.rs#111)//! | Flag | Notes |
[112](https://docs.rs#112)//! |------|-------|
[113](https://docs.rs#113)//! | `tokio` *(default)* | Requires a Tokio runtime |
[114](https://docs.rs#114)//! | `smol` | Uses the smol executor |
[115](https://docs.rs#115)//! | `async-global-executor` | Uses async-global-executor |
[116](https://docs.rs#116)//!
[117](https://docs.rs#117)//! ## TLS backend (pick at most one; `rustls` is the default)
[118](https://docs.rs#118)//!
[119](https://docs.rs#119)//! | Flag | Notes |
[120](https://docs.rs#120)//! |------|-------|
[121](https://docs.rs#121)//! | `rustls` *(default)* | TLS via rustls |
[122](https://docs.rs#122)//! | `native-tls` | TLS via the platform's native library |
[123](https://docs.rs#123)//! | `openssl` | TLS via OpenSSL |
[124](https://docs.rs#124)//!
[125](https://docs.rs#125)//! ## Rustls certificate store (only when `rustls` is active)
[126](https://docs.rs#126)//!
[127](https://docs.rs#127)//! | Flag | Notes |
[128](https://docs.rs#128)//! |------|-------|
[129](https://docs.rs#129)//! | `rustls-platform-verifier` *(default)* | Uses the platform trust store |
[130](https://docs.rs#130)//! | `rustls-native-certs` | Loads native root certificates |
[131](https://docs.rs#131)//! | `rustls-webpki-roots-certs` | Uses the webpki bundled root set |
[132](https://docs.rs#132)//!
[133](https://docs.rs#133)//! ## Rustls crypto provider (at least one must be enabled)
[134](https://docs.rs#134)//!
[135](https://docs.rs#135)//! | Flag | Notes |
[136](https://docs.rs#136)//! |------|-------|
[137](https://docs.rs#137)//! | `rustls--aws_lc_rs` *(default)* | Uses aws-lc-rs |
[138](https://docs.rs#138)//! | `rustls--ring` | Uses ring (more portable) |
[139](https://docs.rs#139)//!
[140](https://docs.rs#140)//! ## Miscellaneous
[141](https://docs.rs#141)//!
[142](https://docs.rs#142)//! | Flag | Notes |
[143](https://docs.rs#143)//! |------|-------|
[144](https://docs.rs#144)//! | `hickory-dns` | Use hickory-dns for name resolution |
[145](https://docs.rs#145)//! | `codegen` | Force code regeneration at build time |
[146](https://docs.rs#146)//! | `verbose-errors` | More detailed AMQP parser error messages |
[147](https://docs.rs#147)

[169](https://docs.rs#169)/// Authentication providers and helpers for connecting to RabbitMQ.

# Connection in lapin - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/lapin/4.10.0/lapin/struct.Connection.html

`pub struct Connection { /* private fields */ }`## Expand description

A TCP connection to the AMQP server.

To connect to the server, one of the [ connect](https://docs.rs/struct.Connection.html#method.connect) methods has to be called.

Afterwards, create a [ Channel](https://docs.rs/struct.Channel.html) by calling

[.](https://docs.rs/struct.Connection.html#method.create_channel)

`create_channel`Also see the RabbitMQ documentation on [connections](https://www.rabbitmq.com/connections.html).

[Source](https://docs.rs/src/lapin/connection.rs.html#83-85)#### pub async fn [connect](https://docs.rs#method.connect)(uri: &[str](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/std/primitive.str.html), options: [ConnectionProperties](https://docs.rs/struct.ConnectionProperties.html)) -> [Result](https://docs.rs/type.Result.html)<Self>

[Source](https://docs.rs/src/lapin/connection.rs.html#83-85)

#### pub async fn [connect](https://docs.rs#method.connect)(uri: &[str](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/std/primitive.str.html), options: [ConnectionProperties](https://docs.rs/struct.ConnectionProperties.html)) -> [Result](https://docs.rs/type.Result.html)<Self>

Connect to an AMQP Server.

The URI must be in the following format:

- `amqp://127.0.0.1:5672`will connect to the default virtual host- `/`.
- `amqp://127.0.0.1:5672/`will connect to the virtual host- `""`(empty string).
- `amqp://127.0.0.1:5672/%2f`will connect to the default virtual host- `/`.

Note that the virtual host has to be escaped with
[URL encoding](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Percent-encoding).

[Source](https://docs.rs/src/lapin/connection.rs.html#161-164)

#### pub async fn [create_channel](https://docs.rs#method.create_channel)(&self) -> [Result](https://docs.rs/type.Result.html)<[Channel](https://docs.rs/struct.Channel.html)>

Open a new [ Channel](https://docs.rs/struct.Channel.html) on this connection.

Channels are lightweight; open one per concurrent logical task. Returns
an error if the connection is not in the [ crate::ConnectionState::Connected](https://docs.rs/enum.ConnectionState.html#variant.Connected)
state or if the channel limit negotiated with the server has been reached.

Block the current thread until the connection is closed.

Useful in simple consumer programs where no other work keeps the process alive. Drops the connection handle then waits for the background IO loop thread to finish.

Perform a graceful AMQP connection close.

Sends `Connection.Close` to the broker and waits for `Connection.Close-Ok`.
`reply_code` should be `200` and `reply_text` `"OK"` for a normal shutdown.
Returns an error if the connection is not in [ crate::ConnectionState::Connected](https://docs.rs/enum.ConnectionState.html#variant.Connected).

# Channel in lapin - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/lapin/4.10.0/lapin/struct.Channel.html

`pub struct Channel { /* private fields */ }`## Expand description

Main entry point for most AMQP operations.

It serves as a lightweight connection and can be obtained from a
[ Connection](https://docs.rs/struct.Connection.html) by calling

[.](https://docs.rs/struct.Connection.html#method.create_channel)

`Connection::create_channel`See also the RabbitMQ documentation on [channels](https://www.rabbitmq.com/channels.html).

[§](https://docs.rs#sharing-channels-across-threads)Sharing channels across threads

The AMQP specification and RabbitMQ both officially discourage sharing a channel across threads: the intent is that each OS thread owns its own channel exclusively.

Rust’s async ecosystem changes the picture. Futures and tasks are *green
threads* that are not pinned to a particular OS thread; work-stealing
executors (such as Tokio’s multi-threaded runtime) can migrate a task to a
different OS thread between any two `.await` points. This means that even
code that never deliberately shares a channel would violate the
one-channel-per-thread rule under a work-stealing executor.

Lapin accounts for this: `Channel` is `Clone + Send + Sync` and all
internal state is protected by the appropriate synchronisation primitives.
It is therefore safe to clone a `Channel` and use the clones from different
tasks — or from different OS threads — concurrently.

## Implementations[§](https://docs.rs#implementations)

[Source](https://docs.rs/src/lapin/channel.rs.html#154-162)#### pub async fn [wait_for_recovery](https://docs.rs#method.wait_for_recovery)(&self, error: [Error](https://docs.rs/struct.Error.html)) -> [Result](https://docs.rs/type.Result.html)<[()](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/std/primitive.unit.html)>

[Source](https://docs.rs/src/lapin/channel.rs.html#154-162)

#### pub async fn [wait_for_recovery](https://docs.rs#method.wait_for_recovery)(&self, error: [Error](https://docs.rs/struct.Error.html)) -> [Result](https://docs.rs/type.Result.html)<[()](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/std/primitive.unit.html)>

Wait for the channel to be recovered after a connection error.

If auto-recovery is enabled and `error` is recoverable, this suspends
the caller until the IO loop has reconnected and replayed the topology.
Returns `Ok(())` when recovery is complete, or re-returns `error` if
recovery is not possible.

Perform a graceful AMQP channel close.

Sends `Channel.Close` and waits for `Channel.Close-Ok`. Use
`reply_code = 200` and `reply_text = "OK"` for a normal shutdown.

[Source](https://docs.rs/src/lapin/channel.rs.html#281-287)#### pub async fn [basic_get](https://docs.rs#method.basic_get)(

[Source](https://docs.rs/src/lapin/channel.rs.html#281-287)

#### pub async fn [basic_get](https://docs.rs#method.basic_get)(
    &self,
    queue: [ShortString](https://docs.rs/amq-protocol-types/10.6.1/x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu/amq_protocol_types/types/struct.ShortString.html),
    options: [BasicGetOptions](https://docs.rs/options/struct.BasicGetOptions.html),
) -> [Result](https://docs.rs/type.Result.html)<[Option](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/core/option/enum.Option.html)<[BasicGetMessage](https://docs.rs/message/struct.BasicGetMessage.html)>>

Synchronously fetch a single message from `queue`.

Returns `None` if the queue is empty, or `Some(``BasicGetMessage``)`.
Unlike [ basic_consume](https://docs.rs/struct.Channel.html#method.basic_consume), this does not establish a long-lived
consumer; it is a one-shot pull. For high-throughput use cases prefer

[.](https://docs.rs/struct.Channel.html#method.basic_consume)

`prefetch_count` controls the maximum number of unacknowledged messages;

whether the limit applies per-consumer (

`false`) or across the whole channel
(`true`).Call this before [ Channel::basic_consume](https://docs.rs/struct.Channel.html#method.basic_consume) to control back-pressure.

    &self,

) -> [Result](https://docs.rs/type.Result.html)<[()](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/std/primitive.unit.html)>

Cancel a consumer subscription.

Tells the server to stop delivering messages for the consumer identified by
`consumer_tag`. This is the counterpart to [ Channel::basic_consume](https://docs.rs/struct.Channel.html#method.basic_consume). After
this call the consumer’s stream will end with

`None`.Prefer calling this over simply dropping the [ Consumer](https://docs.rs/struct.Consumer.html): an explicit cancel
sends the cancellation through the server so that no further messages are
delivered, whereas a drop only discards already-delivered ones.

Publish a message to an exchange.

Routes `payload` through `exchange` using `routing_key`. The empty string
`""` selects the default exchange, which routes messages directly to the
queue whose name matches `routing_key`.

`properties` carries AMQP message metadata (content-type, headers,
delivery-mode, priority, …). Use [ BasicProperties::default()](https://docs.rs/protocol/basic/struct.AMQPProperties.html#method.default) when you
do not need to set any.

Returns a [ crate::PublisherConfirm](https://docs.rs/struct.PublisherConfirm.html) future. If publisher confirms are

**not**enabled (via

[) the future resolves immediately to](https://docs.rs/struct.Channel.html#method.confirm_select)

`Channel::confirm_select`[. If they are enabled, it resolves once the broker acknowledges or negatively-acknowledges the message.](https://docs.rs/enum.Confirmation.html#variant.NotRequested)

`crate::Confirmation::NotRequested`Use [ Channel::wait_for_confirms](https://docs.rs/struct.Channel.html#method.wait_for_confirms) to drain all outstanding confirms at
once.

Bind a source exchange to a destination exchange.

Messages published to `source` that match `routing_key` (and `arguments`
for header exchanges) will be forwarded to `destination`. This is a
RabbitMQ extension that allows exchange-to-exchange routing.

The binding is removed with [ Channel::exchange_unbind](https://docs.rs/struct.Channel.html#method.exchange_unbind).

[Source](https://docs.rs/src/lapin/opt/rustwide/target/x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu/debug/build/lapin-0aa65c3f4b556b6e/out/channel.rs.html#1295-1320)#### pub async fn [exchange_unbind](https://docs.rs#method.exchange_unbind)(

# Consumer in lapin - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/lapin/4.10.0/lapin/struct.Consumer.html

`pub struct Consumer { /* private fields */ }`## Expand description

Continuously consumes message from a Queue.

A consumer represents a stream of messages created from
the [basic.consume](https://www.rabbitmq.com/amqp-0-9-1-quickref.html#basic.consume) AMQP command.
It continuously receives messages from the queue, as opposed to the
[basic.get](https://www.rabbitmq.com/amqp-0-9-1-quickref.html#basic.get) command, which
retrieves only a single message.

A consumer is obtained by calling [ Channel::basic_consume](https://docs.rs/struct.Channel.html#method.basic_consume) with the queue name.

New messages from this consumer can be accessed by obtaining the iterator from the consumer.
This iterator returns new messages and the associated channel in the form of a
[ DeliveryResult](https://docs.rs/message/type.DeliveryResult.html) for as long as the consumer is subscribed to the queue.

It is also possible to set a delegate to be spawned via [ set_delegate](https://docs.rs/struct.Consumer.html#method.set_delegate).

[§](https://docs.rs#message-acknowledgment)Message acknowledgment

There are two ways of acknowledging a message:

- If the flag `BasicConsumeOptions::no_ack``true`while obtaining the consumer from`Channel::basic_consume`
- If the flag `BasicConsumeOptions::no_ack``false`, a message has to be explicitly acknowledged or rejected with`Acker::ack``Acker::nack``Acker::reject``Delivery`

Also see the RabbitMQ documentation about
[Acknowledgement Modes](https://www.rabbitmq.com/consumers.html#acknowledgement-modes).

[§](https://docs.rs#consumer-prefetch)Consumer Prefetch

To limit the maximum number of unacknowledged messages arriving, you can call [ Channel::basic_qos](https://docs.rs/struct.Channel.html#method.basic_qos)
before creating the consumer.

Also see the RabbitMQ documentation about
[Consumer Prefetch](https://www.rabbitmq.com/consumer-prefetch.html).

[§](https://docs.rs#cancel-subscription)Cancel subscription

To stop receiving messages, call [ Channel::basic_cancel](https://docs.rs/struct.Channel.html#method.basic_cancel) with the consumer tag of this
consumer.

[§](https://docs.rs#example)Example

```
use async_rs::{Runtime, traits::*};
use lapin::{options::*, types::FieldTable, Connection, ConnectionProperties, Result};
use futures_lite::stream::StreamExt;
use std::future::Future;
fn main() -> Result<()> {
    let addr = std::env::var("AMQP_ADDR").unwrap_or_else(|_| "amqp://127.0.0.1:5672/%2f".into());
    let runtime = lapin::runtime::default_runtime().unwrap();
    runtime.clone().block_on(async move {
        let conn = Connection::connect_with_runtime(
            &addr,
            ConnectionProperties::default(),
            runtime,
        )
        .await?;
        let channel = conn.create_channel().await?;
        let mut consumer = channel
            .basic_consume(
                "hello".into(),
                "my_consumer".into(),
                BasicConsumeOptions::default(),
                FieldTable::default(),
            )
            .await?;
        while let Some(delivery) = consumer.next().await {
            let delivery = delivery.expect("error in consumer");
            delivery
                .ack(BasicAckOptions::default())
                .await?;
        }
        Ok(())
    })
}
```

# Confirmation in lapin - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/lapin/4.10.0/lapin/enum.Confirmation.html

```
pub enum Confirmation {
    Ack(
```
[Option](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/core/option/enum.Option.html)<[BasicReturnMessage](https://docs.rs/message/struct.BasicReturnMessage.html)>),
    Nack([Option](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/core/option/enum.Option.html)<[BasicReturnMessage](https://docs.rs/message/struct.BasicReturnMessage.html)>),
    NotRequested,
}## Expand description

The broker’s response to a published message.

## Variants[§](https://docs.rs#variants)

[§](https://docs.rs#variant.Ack)

### Ack([Option](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/core/option/enum.Option.html)<[BasicReturnMessage](https://docs.rs/message/struct.BasicReturnMessage.html)>)

The broker acknowledged the message. The inner value carries the returned message if the publish was mandatory/immediate and unroutable.

[§](https://docs.rs#variant.Nack)

### Nack([Option](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/core/option/enum.Option.html)<[BasicReturnMessage](https://docs.rs/message/struct.BasicReturnMessage.html)>)

The broker negatively acknowledged the message (could not route or store it). The inner value carries the returned message if available.

[§](https://docs.rs#variant.NotRequested)

### NotRequested

Publisher confirms were not enabled; the broker did not confirm.

## Implementations[§](https://docs.rs#implementations)

Extract the returned message, if any.

Returns `Some` only when the message was unroutable and returned by the

# ConnectionProperties in lapin - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/lapin/4.10.0/lapin/struct.ConnectionProperties.html

`pub struct ConnectionProperties { /* private fields */ }`## Expand description

Configuration for establishing a [ Connection](https://docs.rs/struct.Connection.html) to the broker.

Build one with [ Default::default](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/core/default/trait.Default.html#tymethod.default) and then chain the

`with_*` / `enable_*`
builder methods to customise it.[§](https://docs.rs#example)Example

```
use lapin::{Connection, ConnectionProperties, Result};
let props = ConnectionProperties::default()
    .with_connection_name("my-app".into())
    .enable_auto_recover();
let conn = Connection::connect("amqp://localhost", props).await?;
```
## Implementations[§](https://docs.rs#implementations)

[Source](https://docs.rs/src/lapin/connection_properties.rs.html#122-131)#### pub fn [enable_auto_recover](https://docs.rs#method.enable_auto_recover)(self) -> Self

[Source](https://docs.rs/src/lapin/connection_properties.rs.html#122-131)

#### pub fn [enable_auto_recover](https://docs.rs#method.enable_auto_recover)(self) -> Self

Enable automatic connection and topology recovery after failures.

When enabled the IO loop will transparently reconnect on network errors
and replay the exchange/queue/binding/consumer topology on the new
connection. Also sets a default TCP reconnect backoff (16 attempts with
exponential delay) unless you have already called [ with_backoff](https://docs.rs/struct.ConnectionProperties.html#method.with_backoff) or

[.](https://docs.rs/struct.ConnectionProperties.html#method.configure_backoff)

`configure_backoff`After catching a recoverable error on a channel, call
[ Channel::wait_for_recovery](https://docs.rs/struct.Channel.html#method.wait_for_recovery) to wait until recovery is complete.

# Acker in lapin - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/lapin/4.10.0/lapin/struct.Acker.html

`pub struct Acker { /* private fields */ }`## Expand description

Handle for acknowledging, negatively acknowledging, or rejecting a delivery.

Obtained from the `acker` field of a [ crate::message::Delivery](https://docs.rs/message/struct.Delivery.html) or by
dereferencing a delivery. Each

`Acker` is single-use: once any of
[,](https://docs.rs/struct.Acker.html#method.ack)

`ack`[, or](https://docs.rs/struct.Acker.html#method.nack)

`nack`[is called the handle is consumed and subsequent calls return](https://docs.rs/struct.Acker.html#method.reject)

`reject``Ok(false)`.If the channel is closed or errored, all outstanding `Acker`s for that
channel are *poisoned* and [ usable](https://docs.rs/struct.Acker.html#method.usable) returns

`false`.## Implementations[§](https://docs.rs#implementations)

[Source](https://docs.rs/src/lapin/acker.rs.html#57-68)#### pub async fn [ack](https://docs.rs#method.ack)(&self, options: [BasicAckOptions](https://docs.rs/options/struct.BasicAckOptions.html)) -> [Result](https://docs.rs/type.Result.html)<[bool](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/std/primitive.bool.html)>

[Source](https://docs.rs/src/lapin/acker.rs.html#57-68)

#### pub async fn [ack](https://docs.rs#method.ack)(&self, options: [BasicAckOptions](https://docs.rs/options/struct.BasicAckOptions.html)) -> [Result](https://docs.rs/type.Result.html)<[bool](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/std/primitive.bool.html)>

Acknowledge the delivery.

Signals to the server that the message has been successfully processed.
Returns `Ok(true)` on success, `Ok(false)` if the acker is already used
or poisoned.

[Source](https://docs.rs/src/lapin/acker.rs.html#76-87)#### pub async fn [nack](https://docs.rs#method.nack)(&self, options: [BasicNackOptions](https://docs.rs/options/struct.BasicNackOptions.html)) -> [Result](https://docs.rs/type.Result.html)<[bool](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/std/primitive.bool.html)>

[Source](https://docs.rs/src/lapin/acker.rs.html#76-87)

#### pub async fn [nack](https://docs.rs#method.nack)(&self, options: [BasicNackOptions](https://docs.rs/options/struct.BasicNackOptions.html)) -> [Result](https://docs.rs/type.Result.html)<[bool](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/std/primitive.bool.html)>

Negatively acknowledge the delivery.

Signals to the server that the message could not be processed. If
[ BasicNackOptions::requeue](https://docs.rs/options/struct.BasicNackOptions.html#structfield.requeue) is

`true` the message is re-queued.
Returns `Ok(true)` on success, `Ok(false)` if the acker is already used
or poisoned.[Source](https://docs.rs/src/lapin/acker.rs.html#95-106)#### pub async fn [reject](https://docs.rs#method.reject)(&self, options: [BasicRejectOptions](https://docs.rs/options/struct.BasicRejectOptions.html)) -> [Result](https://docs.rs/type.Result.html)<[bool](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/std/primitive.bool.html)>

[Source](https://docs.rs/src/lapin/acker.rs.html#95-106)

#### pub async fn [reject](https://docs.rs#method.reject)(&self, options: [BasicRejectOptions](https://docs.rs/options/struct.BasicRejectOptions.html)) -> [Result](https://docs.rs/type.Result.html)<[bool](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/std/primitive.bool.html)>

Reject the delivery.

Signals to the server that the message could not be processed. If
[ BasicRejectOptions::requeue](https://docs.rs/options/struct.BasicRejectOptions.html#structfield.requeue) is

`true` the message is re-queued;
otherwise it is discarded or dead-lettered. Returns `Ok(true)` on
success, `Ok(false)` if the acker is already used or poisoned.## Trait Implementations[§](https://docs.rs#trait-implementations)

# ConnectionBuilder in lapin - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/lapin/4.10.0/lapin/struct.ConnectionBuilder.html

`pub struct ConnectionBuilder<RK: `[RuntimeKit](https://docs.rs/async-rs/0.8.11/x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu/async_rs/traits/runtime/trait.RuntimeKit.html) + [Send](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/core/marker/trait.Send.html) + [Sync](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/core/marker/trait.Sync.html) + [Clone](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/core/clone/trait.Clone.html) + 'static> { /* private fields */ }## Expand description

Builder for [ Connection](https://docs.rs/struct.Connection.html) that collects URI, properties, and TLS config
before connecting.

Use [ DefaultConnectionBuilder::new](https://docs.rs/struct.ConnectionBuilder.html#method.new) for the common case (default runtime).
Use

[to supply a custom runtime.](https://docs.rs/struct.ConnectionBuilder.html#method.new_with_runtime)

`ConnectionBuilder::new_with_runtime`[§](https://docs.rs#example)Example

```
use lapin::{DefaultConnectionBuilder, Result};
let conn = DefaultConnectionBuilder::new()?
    .with_uri_str("amqp://localhost".into())
    .connect()
    .await?;
```

Unlike the synchronous [ TcpStream::into_tls](https://docs.rs/tcp-stream/0.34.14/x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu/tcp_stream/enum.TcpStream.html#method.into_tls), this completes the full handshake
asynchronously and returns

`io::Result<Self>` directly — there is no

# ChannelState in lapin - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/lapin/4.10.0/lapin/enum.ChannelState.html

```
pub enum ChannelState {
    Initial,
    Reconnecting,
    Connected,
    Closing,
    Closed,
    Error,
}
```
## Expand description

The lifecycle state of an AMQP channel.

## Variants[§](https://docs.rs#variants)

[§](https://docs.rs#variant.Initial)

### Initial

The channel has been created but `Channel.Open` has not been sent yet.

[§](https://docs.rs#variant.Reconnecting)

### Reconnecting

The channel is waiting for the connection to be recovered after an error.

[§](https://docs.rs#variant.Connected)

### Connected

The channel is open and ready for AMQP operations.

[§](https://docs.rs#variant.Closing)

### Closing

`Channel.Close` has been sent; waiting for `Channel.Close-Ok`.

[§](https://docs.rs#variant.Closed)

### Closed

The channel has been closed normally.

[§](https://docs.rs#variant.Error)

### Error

The channel has been closed due to a protocol error.

# ConnectionState in lapin - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/lapin/4.10.0/lapin/enum.ConnectionState.html

```
pub enum ConnectionState {
    Initial,
    Connecting,
    Connected,
    Closing,
    Closed,
    Reconnecting,
    Error,
}
```
## Expand description

The lifecycle state of an AMQP connection.

## Variants[§](https://docs.rs#variants)

[§](https://docs.rs#variant.Initial)

### Initial

The connection object has been created but the TCP handshake has not started.

[§](https://docs.rs#variant.Connecting)

### Connecting

The TCP connection is open and the AMQP handshake is in progress.

[§](https://docs.rs#variant.Connected)

### Connected

The AMQP handshake completed successfully; the connection is ready.

[§](https://docs.rs#variant.Closing)

### Closing

`Connection.Close` has been sent; waiting for `Connection.Close-Ok`.

[§](https://docs.rs#variant.Closed)

### Closed

The connection has been closed normally.

[§](https://docs.rs#variant.Reconnecting)

### Reconnecting

The connection was lost and is being re-established (auto-recovery).

[§](https://docs.rs#variant.Error)

### Error

The connection has been closed due to a protocol or IO error.

## Trait Implementations[§](https://docs.rs#trait-implementations)

# ErrorKind in lapin - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/lapin/4.10.0/lapin/enum.ErrorKind.html

```
#[non_exhaustive]pub enum ErrorKind {
```
## Show 14 variants

    ChannelsLimitReached,
    InvalidProtocolVersion([ProtocolVersion](https://docs.rs/amq-protocol/10.6.1/x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu/amq_protocol/frame/structs/struct.ProtocolVersion.html)),
    InvalidChannel([ChannelId](https://docs.rs/amq-protocol-types/10.6.1/x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu/amq_protocol_types/type.ChannelId.html)),
    InvalidChannelState([ChannelState](https://docs.rs/enum.ChannelState.html), &'static [str](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/std/primitive.str.html)),
    InvalidConnectionState([ConnectionState](https://docs.rs/enum.ConnectionState.html)),
    IOError([Arc](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/alloc/sync/struct.Arc.html)<[Error](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/std/io/error/struct.Error.html)>),
    RuntimeShutdownError([Arc](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/alloc/sync/struct.Arc.html)<[Error](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/std/io/error/struct.Error.html)>),
    ParsingError([ParserError](https://docs.rs/amq-protocol-types/10.6.1/x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu/amq_protocol_types/parsing/type.ParserError.html)),
    ProtocolError([AMQPError](https://docs.rs/protocol/struct.AMQPError.html)),
    SerialisationError([Arc](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/alloc/sync/struct.Arc.html)<[GenError](https://docs.rs/cookie-factory/0.3.3/x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu/cookie_factory/internal/enum.GenError.html)>),
    AuthProviderError([String](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/alloc/string/struct.String.html)),
    FutureCompleted,
    NoDefaultRuntime,
    MissingHeartbeatError,
}## Expand description

The type of error that can be returned in this crate.

Even though we expose the complete enumeration of possible error variants, it is not considered stable to exhaustively match on this enumeration: do it at your own risk.

## Variants (Non-exhaustive)[§](https://docs.rs#variants)

## This enum is marked as non-exhaustive

[§](https://docs.rs#variant.ChannelsLimitReached)

### ChannelsLimitReached

The maximum number of channels allowed on this connection has been reached.

[§](https://docs.rs#variant.InvalidProtocolVersion)

### InvalidProtocolVersion([ProtocolVersion](https://docs.rs/amq-protocol/10.6.1/x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu/amq_protocol/frame/structs/struct.ProtocolVersion.html))

The server only supports an AMQP version that this client does not speak.

[§](https://docs.rs#variant.InvalidChannel)

### InvalidChannel([ChannelId](https://docs.rs/amq-protocol-types/10.6.1/x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu/amq_protocol_types/type.ChannelId.html))

An operation was attempted on a channel number that does not exist.

[§](https://docs.rs#variant.InvalidChannelState)

### InvalidChannelState([ChannelState](https://docs.rs/enum.ChannelState.html), &'static [str](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/std/primitive.str.html))

An operation was attempted while the channel was in an incompatible state.

[§](https://docs.rs#variant.InvalidConnectionState)

### InvalidConnectionState([ConnectionState](https://docs.rs/enum.ConnectionState.html))

An operation was attempted while the connection was in an incompatible state.

[§](https://docs.rs#variant.IOError)

An underlying IO error occurred (e.g. connection reset, broken pipe).

[§](https://docs.rs#variant.RuntimeShutdownError)

The async runtime was shut down while an IO operation was in progress.

[§](https://docs.rs#variant.ParsingError)

### ParsingError([ParserError](https://docs.rs/amq-protocol-types/10.6.1/x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu/amq_protocol_types/parsing/type.ParserError.html))

The AMQP frame parser encountered malformed data.

[§](https://docs.rs#variant.ProtocolError)

### ProtocolError([AMQPError](https://docs.rs/protocol/struct.AMQPError.html))

The broker sent an AMQP error (channel or connection level).

[§](https://docs.rs#variant.SerialisationError)

An AMQP frame could not be serialised.

[§](https://docs.rs#variant.AuthProviderError)

### AuthProviderError([String](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/alloc/string/struct.String.html))

The authentication provider returned an error.

[§](https://docs.rs#variant.FutureCompleted)

### FutureCompleted

[§](https://docs.rs#variant.NoDefaultRuntime)

### NoDefaultRuntime

No default async runtime is available (no runtime feature flag was enabled).

[§](https://docs.rs#variant.MissingHeartbeatError)

### MissingHeartbeatError

The broker did not send a heartbeat within the negotiated timeout.

## Trait Implementations[§](https://docs.rs#trait-implementations)

# Event in lapin - Rust

#[non_exhaustive]pub enum Event {
    Connected,
    ConnectionBlocked(
```
[String](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/alloc/string/struct.String.html)),
    ConnectionUnblocked,
    SendFlow([bool](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/std/primitive.bool.html)),
    Error([Error](https://docs.rs/struct.Error.html)),
}## Expand description

## Variants (Non-exhaustive)[§](https://docs.rs#variants)

## This enum is marked as non-exhaustive

[§](https://docs.rs#variant.Connected)

### Connected

The connection has been established (or re-established after recovery).

[§](https://docs.rs#variant.ConnectionBlocked)

### ConnectionBlocked([String](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/alloc/string/struct.String.html))

The broker has blocked the connection due to resource constraints. The inner string is the human-readable reason supplied by the broker.

[§](https://docs.rs#variant.ConnectionUnblocked)

### ConnectionUnblocked

The broker has unblocked the connection.

[§](https://docs.rs#variant.SendFlow)

### SendFlow([bool](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/std/primitive.bool.html))

The broker has changed the allowed flow direction.
`true` means publishing is permitted; `false` means it is paused.

[§](https://docs.rs#variant.Error)

### Error([Error](https://docs.rs/struct.Error.html))

An error occurred on the connection.

# ExchangeKind in lapin - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/lapin/4.10.0/lapin/enum.ExchangeKind.html

```
pub enum ExchangeKind {
    Custom(
```
[String](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/alloc/string/struct.String.html)),
    Direct,
    Fanout,
    Headers,
    Topic,
}## Expand description

## Variants[§](https://docs.rs#variants)

[§](https://docs.rs#variant.Custom)

### Custom([String](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/alloc/string/struct.String.html))

A custom exchange type provided by a broker plugin (e.g. `"x-delayed-message"`).

[§](https://docs.rs#variant.Direct)

### Direct

Routes each message to the queue whose binding key exactly matches the routing key.

[§](https://docs.rs#variant.Fanout)

### Fanout

Routes each message to every bound queue regardless of the routing key.

[§](https://docs.rs#variant.Headers)

### Headers

Routes messages based on header attributes rather than the routing key.

[§](https://docs.rs#variant.Topic)

### Topic

Routes messages using routing key patterns with `*` (one word) and `#` (zero or more words).

# ConsumerDelegate in lapin - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/lapin/4.10.0/lapin/trait.ConsumerDelegate.html

`pub trait ConsumerDelegate: `[Send](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/core/marker/trait.Send.html) + [Sync](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/core/marker/trait.Sync.html) {
    // Required method
    fn [on_new_delivery](https://docs.rs#tymethod.on_new_delivery)(

        delivery: [DeliveryResult](https://docs.rs/message/type.DeliveryResult.html),
    ) -> [Pin](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/core/pin/struct.Pin.html)<[Box](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/alloc/boxed/struct.Box.html)<dyn [Future](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/core/future/future/trait.Future.html)<Output = [()](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/std/primitive.unit.html)> + [Send](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/core/marker/trait.Send.html)>>;

    fn [drop_prefetched_messages](https://docs.rs#method.drop_prefetched_messages)(

}## Expand description

Callback-based alternative to polling a [ Consumer](https://docs.rs/struct.Consumer.html) stream.

Implement this trait and pass your implementation to `Consumer::set_delegate`
to have deliveries dispatched automatically instead of polling the stream.
Any `async Fn(DeliveryResult) -> ()` closure also implements this trait.

## Required Methods[§](https://docs.rs#required-methods)

*In older versions of Rust, dyn compatibility was called "object safety".*

# lapin - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/lapin/latest/lapin/

## Expand description

An async AMQP 0-9-1 client library targeting RabbitMQ.

[§](https://docs.rs#core-concepts)Core concepts

`Connection`

`Channel`[. All AMQP operations (declaring queues, publishing, consuming, …) are performed through channels. Open as many as you need; they are cheap.](https://docs.rs/struct.Connection.html)

`Connection`

`Consumer``Stream` of [values obtained by calling](https://docs.rs/message/struct.Delivery.html)

`message::Delivery`[. Each delivery must be explicitly acknowledged once processed.](https://docs.rs/struct.Channel.html#method.basic_consume)

`Channel::basic_consume`

`PublisherConfirm`[that resolves to a](https://docs.rs/struct.Channel.html#method.basic_publish)

`Channel::basic_publish`[once the broker has acknowledged the message (requires](https://docs.rs/enum.Confirmation.html)

`Confirmation`[).](https://docs.rs/struct.Channel.html#method.confirm_select)

`Channel::confirm_select`[§](https://docs.rs#quick-start)Quick start

```
use async_rs::traits::Executor;
use futures_lite::stream::StreamExt;
use lapin::{
    options::*, types::FieldTable, BasicProperties, Connection,
    ConnectionProperties, Result,
};
fn main() -> Result<()> {
    let addr = std::env::var("AMQP_ADDR")
        .unwrap_or_else(|_| "amqp://127.0.0.1:5672/%2f".into());
    let runtime = lapin::runtime::default_runtime()?;
    runtime.clone().block_on(async move {
        let conn = Connection::connect(&addr, ConnectionProperties::default()).await?;
        let channel = conn.create_channel().await?;
        channel
            .queue_declare("hello".into(), QueueDeclareOptions::durable(), FieldTable::default())
            .await?;
        channel
            .basic_publish(
                "".into(),
                "hello".into(),
                BasicPublishOptions::default(),
                b"Hello, world!",
                BasicProperties::default(),
            )
            .await?
            .await?;
        let mut consumer = channel
            .basic_consume(
                "hello".into(),
                "my_consumer".into(),
                BasicConsumeOptions::default(),
                FieldTable::default(),
            )
            .await?;
        while let Some(delivery) = consumer.next().await {
            let delivery = delivery?;
            delivery.ack(BasicAckOptions::default()).await?;
        }
        Ok(())
    })
}
```
[§](https://docs.rs#automatic-connection-recovery)Automatic connection recovery

Enable recovery in [ ConnectionProperties](https://docs.rs/struct.ConnectionProperties.html) to automatically reconnect and
replay topology (exchanges, queues, bindings, consumers) after a network
failure:

```
use lapin::ConnectionProperties;
let props = ConnectionProperties::default().enable_auto_recover();
// then pass `props` to Connection::connect(…)
```
After catching an error from a channel operation, call
[ Channel::wait_for_recovery](https://docs.rs/struct.Channel.html#method.wait_for_recovery) to block until the connection has been
re-established:

`channel.wait_for_recovery(error).await?;`[§](https://docs.rs#feature-flags)Feature flags

[§](https://docs.rs#async-runtime-pick-exactly-one)Async runtime (pick exactly one)

| Flag | Notes |
|---|---|
| `tokio`(default) | Requires a Tokio runtime |
| `smol` | Uses the smol executor |
| `async-global-executor` | Uses async-global-executor |

[§](https://docs.rs#tls-backend-pick-at-most-one-rustls-is-the-default)TLS backend (pick at most one; `rustls` is the default)

| Flag | Notes |
|---|---|
| `rustls`(default) | TLS via rustls |
| `native-tls` | TLS via the platform’s native library |
| `openssl` | TLS via OpenSSL |

[§](https://docs.rs#rustls-certificate-store-only-when-rustls-is-active)Rustls certificate store (only when `rustls` is active)

| Flag | Notes |
|---|---|
| `rustls-platform-verifier`(default) | Uses the platform trust store |
| `rustls-native-certs` | Loads native root certificates |
| `rustls-webpki-roots-certs` | Uses the webpki bundled root set |

[§](https://docs.rs#rustls-crypto-provider-at-least-one-must-be-enabled)Rustls crypto provider (at least one must be enabled)

| Flag | Notes |
|---|---|
| `rustls--aws_lc_rs`(default) | Uses aws-lc-rs |
| `rustls--ring` | Uses ring (more portable) |

[§](https://docs.rs#miscellaneous)Miscellaneous

| Flag | Notes |
|---|---|
| `hickory-dns` | Use hickory-dns for name resolution |
| `codegen` | Force code regeneration at build time |
| `verbose-errors` | More detailed AMQP parser error messages |

## Re-exports[§](https://docs.rs#reexports)

## Modules[§](https://docs.rs#modules)

- [auth](https://docs.rs/auth/index.html)
- Authentication providers and helpers for connecting to RabbitMQ.
- [message](https://docs.rs/message/index.html)
- AMQP message types delivered to consumers.
- [options](https://docs.rs/options/index.html)
- Options structs for every AMQP method that accepts flag arguments.
- [protocol](https://docs.rs/protocol/index.html)
- Code-generated AMQP 0-9-1 method and property types derived from the RabbitMQ spec.
- [runtime](https://docs.rs/runtime/index.html)
- Runtime selection and helpers.

## Structs[§](https://docs.rs#structs)

- [Acker](https://docs.rs/struct.Acker.html)
- Handle for acknowledging, negatively acknowledging, or rejecting a delivery.
- [Channel](https://docs.rs/struct.Channel.html)
- Main entry point for most AMQP operations.
- [Channel](https://docs.rs/struct.ChannelStatus.html)- Status
- Shared, cheaply cloneable view of a channel’s current state.
- [Configuration](https://docs.rs/struct.Configuration.html)
- The negotiated connection parameters returned by the AMQP handshake.
- [Connection](https://docs.rs/struct.Connection.html)
- A TCP connection to the AMQP server.
- [Connection](https://docs.rs/struct.ConnectionBuilder.html)- Builder
- Builder for `Connection`

**AMQP 0-9-1 protocol codec and TCP/TLS connection layer for Rust.**

This workspace provides the low-level AMQP 0-9-1 building blocks used by
[lapin](https://docs.rs/lapin). It is split into focused sub-crates that can

## Crates in this workspace

Most users should depend on `amq-protocol` directly — it re-exports everything
and wires up the sub-crates. Depend on a sub-crate only when you need a strict
subset of the functionality.

## Feature flags

### Async runtime (pick exactly one)

| Flag | Notes |
| `tokio`*(default)* | Requires a running Tokio runtime |
| `smol` | Uses the smol executor |
| `async-global-executor` | Uses async-global-executor |

### TLS backend (pick at most one)

| Flag | Notes |
| `rustls`*(default)* | TLS via rustls |
| `native-tls` | TLS via the platform's native library |
| `openssl` | TLS via OpenSSL |

### Rustls certificate store (when `rustls` is active)

| Flag | Notes |
| `rustls-platform-verifier`*(default)* | Uses the platform trust store |
| `rustls-native-certs` | Loads native root certificates |
| `rustls-webpki-roots-certs` | Uses the webpki bundled root set |

### Rustls crypto provider (at least one required)

| Flag | Notes |
| `rustls--aws_lc_rs`*(default)* | Uses aws-lc-rs |
| `rustls--ring` | Uses ring (more portable, e.g. builds on Windows) |

| Flag | Notes |
| `codegen` | Force protocol code regeneration at build time |
| `verbose-errors` | More detailed AMQP parser error messages |

# async-trait 0.1.89 - Docs.rs

Source: https://docs.rs/crate/async-trait/^0.1.42

# Async trait methods

The stabilization of async functions in traits in Rust 1.75 did not include
support for using traits containing async functions as `dyn Trait`. Trying to
use dyn with an async trait produces the following error:

```
```
```
error[E0038]: the trait `Trait` is not dyn compatible
 --> src/main.rs:5:22
  |
5 | pub fn make() -> Box<dyn Trait> {
  |                      ^^^^^^^^^ `Trait` is not dyn compatible
  |
note: for a trait to be dyn compatible it needs to allow building a vtable
      for more information, visit <https://doc.rust-lang.org/reference/items/traits.html#dyn-compatibility>
 --> src/main.rs:2:14
  |
1 | pub trait Trait {
  |           ----- this trait is not dyn compatible...
2 |     async fn f(&self);
  |              ^ ...because method `f` is `async`
  = help: consider moving `f` to another trait
```
This crate provides an attribute macro to make async fn in traits work with dyn traits.

Please refer to [ why async fn in traits are hard](https://smallcultfollowing.com/babysteps/blog/2019/10/26/async-fn-in-traits-are-hard/) for a deeper analysis
of how this implementation differs from what the compiler and language deliver
natively.

## Example

This example implements the core of a highly effective advertising platform using async fn in a trait.

The only thing to notice here is that we write an `#[async_trait]` macro on top
of traits and trait impls that contain async fn, and then they work. We get to
have `Vec<Box<dyn Advertisement + Sync>>` or `&[&dyn Advertisement]`, for
example.

```
use async_trait;
;
```
## Supported features

It is the intention that all features of Rust traits should work nicely with
#[async_trait], but the edge cases are numerous. *Please file an issue if you
see unexpected borrow checker errors, type errors, or warnings.* There is no use
of `unsafe` in the expanded code, so rest assured that if your code compiles it
can't be that badly broken.

- 👍 Self by value, by reference, by mut reference, or no self;
- 👍 Any number of arguments, any return value;
- 👍 Generic type parameters and lifetime parameters;
- 👍 Associated types;
- 👍 Having async and non-async functions in the same trait;
- 👍 Default implementations provided by the trait;
- 👍 Elided lifetimes.

## Explanation

Async fns get transformed into methods that return `Pin<Box<dyn Future + Send + 'async_trait>>` and delegate to an async block.

For example the `impl Advertisement for AutoplayingVideo` above would be
expanded as:

```
```
## Non-threadsafe futures

Not all async traits need futures that are `dyn Future + Send`. To avoid having
Send and Sync bounds placed on the async trait methods, invoke the async trait
macro as `#[async_trait(?Send)]` on both the trait and the impl blocks.

## Elided lifetimes

Be aware that async fn syntax does not allow lifetime elision outside of `&` and
`&mut` references. (This is true even when not using #[async_trait].)
Lifetimes must be named or marked by the placeholder `'_`.

Fortunately the compiler is able to diagnose missing lifetimes with a good error message.

```
type Elided<'a> = &'a usize;
```
```
error[E0726]: implicit elided lifetime not allowed here
 --> src/main.rs:9:29
  |
9 |     async fn test(not_okay: Elided, okay: &usize) {}
  |                             ^^^^^^- help: indicate the anonymous lifetime: `<'_>`
```
The fix is to name the lifetime or use `'_`.

```
```

# backon 1.6.0 - Docs.rs

Source: https://docs.rs/crate/backon/^1.6

Make **retry** like a built-in feature provided by Rust.

- **Simple API**: Native feel:- `your_fn.retry(ExponentialBuilder::default()).await`.
- **Sync & Async**: Supports both blocking and async operations seamlessly.
- **Precise Control**: Define when to retry and get notified via- `when`- `notify`
- **Custom Strategies**: Use built-in backoff strategies (exponential, constant) or define custom ones. Also supports dynamic backoff, such as using the HTTP- `Retry-After`header.
- **Cross-Platform**: Works everywhere Rust does, including- `wasm`&- `no-std`.

## Quick Start

For more examples, check out the [examples](https://docs.rs/backon/latest/backon/docs/examples/index.html).

### Retry an async function.

```
use Result;
use ExponentialBuilder;
use Retryable;
async
async
```
### Retry a blocking function.

```
use Result;
use BlockingRetryable;
use ExponentialBuilder;
```

# event-listener 5.4.1 - Docs.rs

Source: https://docs.rs/crate/event-listener/^5.0

# event-listener

Notify async tasks or threads.

This is a synchronization primitive similar to [eventcounts](https://www.1024cores.net/home/lock-free-algorithms/eventcounts) invented by Dmitry Vyukov.

You can use this crate to turn non-blocking data structures into async or blocking data
structures. See a [simple mutex](https://docs.rs/examples/mutex.rs) implementation that exposes an async and a blocking interface
for acquiring locks.

## Examples

Wait until another thread sets a boolean flag:

```
use ;
use Arc;
use thread;
use Duration;
use Event;
let flag = new;
let event = new;
// Spawn a thread that will set the flag after 1 second.
spawn;
// Wait until the flag is set.
loop
```

# flume 0.12.0 - Docs.rs

Source: https://docs.rs/crate/flume/^0.12

# Flume

A blazingly fast multi-producer, multi-consumer channel.

```
use thread;
```
## Why Flume?

- **Featureful**: Unbounded, bounded and rendezvous queues
- **Fast**: Always faster than- `std::sync::mpsc`and sometimes- `crossbeam-channel`
- **Safe**: No- `unsafe`code anywhere in the codebase!
- **Flexible**:- `Sender`and- `Receiver`both implement- `Send + Sync + Clone`
- **Familiar**: Drop-in replacement for- `std::sync::mpsc`
- **Capable**: Additional features like MPMC support and send timeouts/deadlines
- **Simple**: Few dependencies, minimal codebase, fast to compile
- **Asynchronous**:- `async`support, including mix 'n match with sync code
- **Ergonomic**: Powerful- `select`-like interface

## Usage

To use Flume, place the following line under the `[dependencies]` section in your `Cargo.toml`:

```
 = "x.y"
```
## Cargo Features

Flume comes with several optional features:

-
`spin`: use spinlocks instead of OS-level synchronisation primitives internally for some kind of data access (may be more performant on a small number of platforms for specific workloads)
-
`select`: Adds support for the`Selector`
-
`async`: Adds support for the[async API](https://docs.rs/flume/latest/flume/async/index.html), including on otherwise synchronous channels
-
`eventual-fairness`: Use randomness in the implementation of`Selector`to avoid biasing/saturating certain events over others

You can enable these features by changing the dependency in your `Cargo.toml` like so:

```
 = {  = "x.y",  = false,  = ["async", "select"] }
```
Although Flume has its own extensive benchmarks, don't take it from here that Flume is quick.
The following graph is from the `crossbeam-channel` benchmark suite.

Tests were performed on an AMD Ryzen 7 3700x with 8/16 cores running Linux kernel 5.11.2 with the bfq scheduler.

## Status

Flume is in [casual maintenance mode](https://casuallymaintained.tech/). This means that the crate will continue to
receive critical security and bug fixes, but heavy feature development has stopped. If you're looking for a new
feature, you're welcome to open a PR and I'll try to find the time to review it.

Flume has been great fun to work on, and I'm happy that it's being used successfully by so many people. I consider the crate to be largely feature-complete at this point (bar small details here and there).

## License

Flume is licensed under either of:

-
Apache License 2.0, ( [http://www.apache.org/licenses/LICENSE-2.0](http://www.apache.org/licenses/LICENSE-2.0))
-
MIT license ( [http://opensource.org/licenses/MIT](http://opensource.org/licenses/MIT))

# tracing 0.1.44 - Docs.rs

Source: https://docs.rs/crate/tracing/^0.1

# tracing

Application-level tracing for Rust.

## Overview

`tracing` is a framework for instrumenting Rust programs to collect
structured, event-based diagnostic information.

In asynchronous systems like Tokio, interpreting traditional log messages can
often be quite challenging. Since individual tasks are multiplexed on the same
thread, associated events and log lines are intermixed making it difficult to
trace the logic flow. `tracing` expands upon logging-style diagnostics by
allowing libraries and applications to record structured events with additional
information about *temporality* and *causality* — unlike a log message, a span
in `tracing` has a beginning and end time, may be entered and exited by the
flow of execution, and may exist within a nested tree of similar spans. In
addition, `tracing` spans are *structured*, with the ability to record typed
data as well as textual messages.

The `tracing` crate provides the APIs necessary for instrumenting libraries
and applications to emit trace data.

*Compiler support:  requires *

`rustc` 1.65+## Usage

(The examples below are borrowed from the `log` crate's yak-shaving
[example](https://docs.rs/log/0.4.10/log/index.html#examples), modified to
idiomatic `tracing`.)

### In Applications

In order to record trace events, executables have to use a `Subscriber`
implementation compatible with `tracing`. A `Subscriber` implements a way of
collecting trace data, such as by logging it to standard output. [ tracing_subscriber](https://docs.rs/tracing-subscriber/)'s

[provides reasonable defaults. Additionally,](https://docs.rs/tracing-subscriber/0.3/tracing_subscriber/fmt/index.html)

`fmt` module`tracing-subscriber` is able to consume messages emitted by `log`-instrumented libraries and modules.The simplest way to use a subscriber is to call the `set_global_default` function.

```
use ;
use FmtSubscriber;
```
```
[]
 = "0.1"
 = "0.3.0"
```
This subscriber will be used as the default in all threads for the remainder of the duration
of the program, similar to how loggers work in the `log` crate.

In addition, you can locally override the default subscriber. For example:

```
use ;
use FmtSubscriber;
```
This approach allows trace data to be collected by multiple subscribers within different contexts in the program. Note that the override only applies to the currently executing thread; other threads will not see the change from with_default.

Any trace events generated outside the context of a subscriber will not be collected.

Once a subscriber has been set, instrumentation points may be added to the
executable using the `tracing` crate's macros.

### In Libraries

Libraries should only rely on the `tracing` crate and use the provided macros
and types to collect whatever information might be useful to downstream consumers.

```
use ;
use ;
// the `#[tracing::instrument]` attribute creates and enters a span
// every time the instrumented function is called. The span is named after the
// the function or method. Parameters passed to the function are recorded as fields.
```
```
[]
 = "0.1"
```
Note: Libraries should *NOT* call `set_global_default()`, as this will cause
conflicts when executables try to set the default later.

### In Asynchronous Code

If you are instrumenting code that make use of
[ std::future::Future](https://doc.rust-lang.org/stable/std/future/trait.Future.html)
or async/await, avoid using the

`Span::enter` method. The following example
*will not*work:

```
async
```
```
async
```
The span guard `_s` will not exit until the future generated by the `async` block is complete.
Since futures and spans can be entered and exited *multiple* times without them completing,
the span remains entered for as long as the future exists, rather than being entered only when
it is polled, leading to very confusing and incorrect output.
For more details, see [the documentation on closing spans](https://tracing.rs/tracing/span/index.html#closing-spans).

There are two ways to instrument asynchronous code. The first is through the
[ Future::instrument](https://docs.rs/tracing/latest/tracing/trait.Instrument.html#method.instrument) combinator:

```
use Instrument;
let my_future = async ;
my_future
    .instrument
    .await
```
`Future::instrument` attaches a span to the future, ensuring that the span's lifetime
is as long as the future's.

The second, and preferred, option is through the
[ #[instrument]](https://docs.rs/tracing/0.1.44/tracing/attr.instrument.html)
attribute:

```
use ;
use ;
use io;
async
```
Under the hood, the `#[instrument]` macro performs the same explicit span
attachment that `Future::instrument` does.

### Concepts

This crate provides macros for creating `Span`s and `Event`s, which represent
periods of time and momentary events within the execution of a program,
respectively.

As a rule of thumb, *spans* should be used to represent discrete units of work
(e.g., a given request's lifetime in a server) or periods of time spent in a
given context (e.g., time spent interacting with an instance of an external
system, such as a database). In contrast, *events* should be used to represent
points in time within a span — a request returned with a given status code,
*n* new items were taken from a queue, and so on.

`Span`s are constructed using the `span!` macro, and then *entered*
to indicate that some code takes place within the context of that `Span`:

```
use ;
// Construct a new span named "my span".
let mut span = span!;
span.in_scope;
// Dropping the span will close it, indicating that it has ended.
```
The [ #[instrument]](https://docs.rs/tracing/0.1.44/tracing/attr.instrument.html) attribute macro
can reduce some of this boilerplate:

```
use ;
```
The `Event` type represent an event that occurs instantaneously, and is
essentially a `Span` that cannot be entered. They are created using the `event!`
macro:

```
use ;
event!;
```
Users of the [ log](https://docs.rs/log/0.4.6/log/) crate should note that

`tracing` exposes a set of macros for
creating `Event`s (`trace!`, `debug!`, `info!`, `warn!`, and `error!`) which may
be invoked with the same syntax as the similarly-named macros from the `log`
crate. Often, the process of converting a project to use `tracing` can begin
with a simple drop-in replacement.## Supported Rust Versions

Tracing is built against the latest stable release. The minimum supported version is 1.42. The current Tracing version is not guaranteed to build on Rust versions earlier than the minimum supported version.

Tracing follows the same compiler support policies as the rest of the Tokio project. The current stable Rust compiler and the three most recent minor versions before it will always be supported. For example, if the current stable compiler version is 1.45, the minimum supported version will not be increased past 1.42, three minor versions prior. Increasing the minimum supported compiler version is not considered a semver breaking change as long as doing so complies with this policy.

## Ecosystem

### Related Crates

In addition to `tracing` and `tracing-core`, the [ tokio-rs/tracing](https://github.com/tokio-rs/tracing) repository
contains several additional crates designed to be used with the

`tracing` ecosystem.
This includes a collection of `Subscriber` implementations, as well as utility
and adapter crates to assist in writing `Subscriber`s and instrumenting
applications.In particular, the following crates are likely to be of interest:

- `tracing-futures`- `futures`crate, allowing spans to be attached to- `Future`s,- `Stream`s, and- `Executor`s.
- `tracing-subscriber`- `Subscriber`implementations and utilities for working with- `Subscriber`s. This includes a- `FmtSubscriber`- `FmtSubscriber`for logging formatted trace data to stdout, with similar filtering and formatting to the- `env_logger`
- `tracing-log`- `log`- `tracing`- `Event`s within the trace tree. This is useful when a project using- `tracing`have dependencies which use- `log`. Note that if you're using- `tracing-subscriber`'s- `FmtSubscriber`, you don't need to depend on- `tracing-log`directly.

Additionally, there are also several third-party crates which are not
maintained by the `tokio` project. These include:

- `tracing-timing`- `tracing`. It provides a subscriber that records the time elapsed between pairs of- `tracing`events and generates histograms.
- `tracing-opentelemetry`- [OpenTelemetry](https://opentelemetry.io/)-compatible distributed tracing systems.
- `tracing-honeycomb`- [honeycomb.io](https://www.honeycomb.io/). Backed by- `tracing-distributed`
- `tracing-distributed`
- `tracing-actix`- `tracing`integration for the- `actix`actor framework.
- `axum-insights`- `tracing`integration and Application insights export for the- `axum`web framework.
- `tracing-gelf`
- `tracing-coz`- [coz](https://github.com/plasma-umass/coz)causal profiler (Linux-only).
- `test-log`- `tracing`for tests, based on environment variables with an- `env_logger`compatible syntax.
- `tracing-unwrap`- `Result`or- `Option`types to a- `Subscriber`.
- `diesel-tracing`- `diesel`
- `tracing-tracy`- [Tracy](https://github.com/wolfpld/tracy)profiles in instrumented applications.
- `tracing-elastic-apm`- [Elastic APM](https://www.elastic.co/apm).
- `tracing-etw`- [ETW](https://docs.microsoft.com/en-us/windows/win32/etw/about-event-tracing)events.
- `tracing-fluent-assertions`- `tracing`spans.
- `sentry-tracing`- [Sentry](https://sentry.io/welcome/).
- `tracing-loki`- [Grafana Loki](https://grafana.com/oss/loki/).
- `tracing-logfmt`
- `json-subscriber`- `FmtSubscriber`

If you're the maintainer of a `tracing` ecosystem crate not listed above,
please let us know! We'd love to add your project to the list!

**Note:** that some of the ecosystem crates are currently unreleased and
undergoing active development. They may be less stable than `tracing` and
`tracing-core`.

## Supported Rust Versions

Tracing is built against the latest stable release. The minimum supported version is 1.65. The current Tracing version is not guaranteed to build on Rust versions earlier than the minimum supported version.

Tracing follows the same compiler support policies as the rest of the Tokio project. The current stable Rust compiler and the three most recent minor versions before it will always be supported. For example, if the current stable compiler version is 1.69, the minimum supported version will not be increased past 1.66, three minor versions prior. Increasing the minimum supported compiler version is not considered a semver breaking change as long as doing so complies with this policy.

# futures-lite 2.6.1 - Docs.rs

Source: https://docs.rs/crate/futures-lite/^2.0

# futures-lite

A lightweight async prelude.

This crate is a subset of [futures](https://docs.rs/futures) that compiles an order of magnitude faster, fixes minor
warts in its API, fills in some obvious gaps, and removes almost all unsafe code from it.

In short, this crate aims to be more enjoyable than [futures](https://docs.rs/futures) but still fully compatible with
it.

The API for this crate is intentionally constrained. Please consult the
[features list](https://github.com/smol-rs/futures-lite/blob/master/FEATURES.md) for APIs that are occluded from this crate.

## Examples

```
use future;
```

# serde_json 1.0.150 - Docs.rs

Source: https://docs.rs/crate/serde_json/^1.0

**Serde is a framework for  serializing and deserializing Rust data structures efficiently and generically.**

```
[]
 = "1.0"
```
You may be looking for:

- [JSON API documentation](https://docs.rs/serde_json)
- [Serde API documentation](https://docs.rs/serde)
- [Detailed documentation about Serde](https://serde.rs/)
- [Setting up](https://serde.rs/derive.html)- `#[derive(Serialize, Deserialize)]`
- [Release notes](https://github.com/serde-rs/json/releases)

JSON is a ubiquitous open-standard format that uses human-readable text to transmit data objects consisting of key-value pairs.

```
```
There are three common ways that you might find yourself needing to work with JSON data in Rust.

- **As text data.**An unprocessed string of JSON data that you receive on an HTTP endpoint, read from a file, or prepare to send to a remote server.
- **As an untyped or loosely typed representation.**Maybe you want to check that some JSON data is valid before passing it on, but without knowing the structure of what it contains. Or you want to do very basic manipulations like insert a key in a particular spot.
- **As a strongly typed Rust data structure.**When you expect all or most of your data to conform to a particular structure and want to get real work done without JSON's loosey-goosey nature tripping you up.

Serde JSON provides efficient, flexible, safe ways of converting data between each of these representations.

## Operating on untyped JSON values

Any valid JSON data can be manipulated in the following recursive enum
representation. This data structure is [ serde_json::Value](https://docs.rs/serde_json/1/serde_json/value/enum.Value.html).

```
```
A string of JSON data can be parsed into a `serde_json::Value` by the
[ serde_json::from_str](https://docs.rs/serde_json/1/serde_json/de/fn.from_str.html) function. There is also

[for parsing from a byte slice](https://docs.rs/serde_json/1/serde_json/de/fn.from_slice.html)

`from_slice``&[u8]` and
[for parsing from any](https://docs.rs/serde_json/1/serde_json/de/fn.from_reader.html)

`from_reader``io::Read` like a File or a
TCP stream.```
use ;
```
The result of square bracket indexing like `v["name"]` is a borrow of the data
at that index, so the type is `&Value`. A JSON map can be indexed with string
keys, while a JSON array can be indexed with integer keys. If the type of the
data is not right for the type with which it is being indexed, or if a map does
not contain the key being indexed, or if the index into a vector is out of
bounds, the returned element is `Value::Null`.

When a `Value` is printed, it is printed as a JSON string. So in the code above,
the output looks like `Please call "John Doe" at the number "+44 1234567"`. The
quotation marks appear because `v["name"]` is a `&Value` containing a JSON
string and its JSON representation is `"John Doe"`. Printing as a plain string
without quotation marks involves converting from a JSON string to a Rust string
with [ as_str()](https://docs.rs/serde_json/1/serde_json/enum.Value.html#method.as_str) or avoiding the use of

`Value` as described in the following
section.The `Value` representation is sufficient for very basic tasks but can be tedious
to work with for anything more significant. Error handling is verbose to
implement correctly, for example imagine trying to detect the presence of
unrecognized fields in the input data. The compiler is powerless to help you
when you make a mistake, for example imagine typoing `v["name"]` as `v["nmae"]`
in one of the dozens of places it is used in your code.

## Parsing JSON as strongly typed data structures

Serde provides a powerful way of mapping JSON data into Rust data structures largely automatically.

```
use ;
use Result;
```
This is the same `serde_json::from_str` function as before, but this time we
assign the return value to a variable of type `Person` so Serde will
automatically interpret the input data as a `Person` and produce informative
error messages if the layout does not conform to what a `Person` is expected to
look like.

Any type that implements Serde's `Deserialize` trait can be deserialized this
way. This includes built-in Rust standard library types like `Vec<T>` and
`HashMap<K, V>`, as well as any structs or enums annotated with
`#[derive(Deserialize)]`.

Once we have `p` of type `Person`, our IDE and the Rust compiler can help us use
it correctly like they do for any other Rust code. The IDE can autocomplete
field names to prevent typos, which was impossible in the `serde_json::Value`
representation. And the Rust compiler can check that when we write
`p.phones[0]`, then `p.phones` is guaranteed to be a `Vec<String>` so indexing
into it makes sense and produces a `String`.

The necessary setup for using Serde's derive macros is explained on the * Using
derive* page of the Serde site.

## Constructing JSON values

Serde JSON provides a [ json! macro](https://docs.rs/serde_json/1/serde_json/macro.json.html) to build

`serde_json::Value`
objects with very natural JSON syntax.```
use json;
```
The `Value::to_string()` function converts a `serde_json::Value` into a `String`
of JSON text.

One neat thing about the `json!` macro is that variables and expressions can be
interpolated directly into the JSON value as you are building it. Serde will
check at compile time that the value you are interpolating is able to be
represented as JSON.

```
let full_name = "John Doe";
let age_last_year = 42;
// The type of `john` is `serde_json::Value`
let john = json!;
```
This is amazingly convenient, but we have the problem we had before with
`Value`: the IDE and Rust compiler cannot help us if we get it wrong. Serde JSON
provides a better way of serializing strongly-typed data structures into JSON
text.

## Creating JSON by serializing data structures

A data structure can be converted to a JSON string by
[ serde_json::to_string](https://docs.rs/serde_json/1/serde_json/ser/fn.to_string.html). There is also

[which serializes to a](https://docs.rs/serde_json/1/serde_json/ser/fn.to_vec.html)

`serde_json::to_vec``Vec<u8>` and
[which serializes to any](https://docs.rs/serde_json/1/serde_json/ser/fn.to_writer.html)

`serde_json::to_writer``io::Write`
such as a File or a TCP stream.```
use ;
use Result;
```
Any type that implements Serde's `Serialize` trait can be serialized this way.
This includes built-in Rust standard library types like `Vec<T>` and `HashMap<K, V>`, as well as any structs or enums annotated with `#[derive(Serialize)]`.

## Performance

It is fast. You should expect in the ballpark of 500 to 1000 megabytes per
second deserialization and 600 to 900 megabytes per second serialization,
depending on the characteristics of your data. This is competitive with the
fastest C and C++ JSON libraries or even 30% faster for many use cases.
Benchmarks live in the [serde-rs/json-benchmark](https://github.com/serde-rs/json-benchmark) repo.

## Getting help

Serde is one of the most widely used Rust libraries, so any place that
Rustaceans congregate will be able to help you out. For chat, consider trying
the [#rust-questions](https://discord.com/channels/273534239310479360/274215136414400513) or [#rust-beginners](https://discord.com/channels/273534239310479360/273541522815713281) channels of the unofficial community
Discord (invite: [https://discord.gg/rust-lang-community](https://discord.gg/rust-lang-community)), the [#rust-usage](https://discord.com/channels/442252698964721669/443150878111694848) or
[#beginners](https://discord.com/channels/442252698964721669/448238009733742612) channels of the official Rust Project Discord (invite:
[https://discord.gg/rust-lang](https://discord.gg/rust-lang)), or the [#general](https://rust-lang.zulipchat.com/#narrow/stream/122651-general) stream in Zulip. For
asynchronous, consider the [[rust] tag on StackOverflow](https://stackoverflow.com/questions/tagged/rust), the
[/r/rust](https://www.reddit.com/r/rust) subreddit which has a pinned weekly easy questions post, or the Rust
[Discourse forum](https://users.rust-lang.org). It's acceptable to file a support issue in this
repo, but they tend not to get as many eyes as any of the above and may get
closed without a response after some time.

## No-std support

As long as there is a memory allocator, it is possible to use serde_json without the rest of the Rust standard library. Disable the default "std" feature and enable the "alloc" feature:

```
[]
 = {  = "1.0",  = false,  = ["alloc"] }
```
For JSON support in Serde without a memory allocator, please see the
[ serde-json-core](https://github.com/rust-embedded-community/serde-json-core) crate.

# smol 2.0.2 - Docs.rs

Source: https://docs.rs/crate/smol/^2.0

# smol

A small and fast async runtime.

This crate simply re-exports other smaller async crates (see the source).

To use tokio-based libraries with smol, apply the [ async-compat](https://docs.rs/async-compat/latest/async_compat/) adapter to futures and I/O
types.

See the [ smol-macros](https://docs.rs/smol-macros/latest/smol_macros/) crate if you want a no proc-macro, fast compiling, easy-to-use
async main and/or multi-threaded Executor setup out of the box.

## Examples

Connect to an HTTP website, make a GET request, and pipe the response to the standard output:

```
use ;
```
There's a lot more in the [examples](https://github.com/smol-rs/smol/tree/master/examples) directory.

## Subcrates

- [async-channel](https://github.com/smol-rs/async-channel)- Multi-producer multi-consumer channels
- [async-executor](https://github.com/smol-rs/async-executor)- Composable async executors
- [async-fs](https://github.com/smol-rs/async-fs)- Async filesystem primitives
- [async-io](https://github.com/smol-rs/async-io)- Async adapter for I/O types, also timers
- [async-lock](https://github.com/smol-rs/async-lock)- Async locks (barrier, mutex, reader-writer lock, semaphore)
- [async-net](https://github.com/smol-rs/async-net)- Async networking primitives (TCP/UDP/Unix)
- [async-process](https://github.com/smol-rs/async-process)- Async interface for working with processes
- [async-task](https://github.com/smol-rs/async-task)- Task abstraction for building executors
- [blocking](https://github.com/smol-rs/blocking)- A thread pool for blocking I/O
- [futures-lite](https://github.com/smol-rs/futures-lite)- A lighter fork of- [futures](https://github.com/rust-lang/futures-rs)
- [polling](https://github.com/smol-rs/polling)- Portable interface to epoll, kqueue, event ports, and wepoll

## TLS certificate

Some code examples are using TLS for authentication. The repository
contains a self-signed certificate usable for testing, but it should **not**
be used for real-world scenarios. Browsers and tools like curl will
show this certificate as insecure.

In browsers, accept the security prompt or use `curl -k` on the
command line to bypass security warnings.

The certificate file was generated using
[minica](https://github.com/jsha/minica) and
[openssl](https://www.openssl.org/):

```
minica --domains localhost -ip-addresses 127.0.0.1 -ca-cert certificate.pem
openssl pkcs12 -export -out identity.pfx -inkey localhost/key.pem -in localhost/cert.pem
```
Another useful tool for making certificates is [mkcert](https://github.com/FiloSottile/mkcert).

## MSRV Policy

The Minimum Supported Rust Version (MSRV) of this crate is **1.63**. As a **tentative** policy, the MSRV will not advance past the [current Rust version provided by Debian Stable](https://packages.debian.org/stable/rust/rustc). At the time of writing, this version of Rust is *1.63*. However, the MSRV may be advanced further in the event of a major ecosystem shift or a security vulnerability.
